content: It is crucial for future research to include the surveillance of pre-treatment integrase resistance and to focus on optimizing drug resistance monitoring. The availability of assays for detecting acute HIV infection, such as HIV-antigen immunoassays, fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody immunoassays, and nucleic acid testing (NAT), remains limited in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) where CAB-LA might be offered. Evidence supporting the clinical and public health utility of these assays is less robust compared to the use of national validated testing algorithms, which typically rely on rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). For oral PrEP, same-day initiation has been a key factor in improving access and uptake. However, the use of NAT, which often requires referral to external laboratories, sample transportation, and processing time, may hinder same-day initiation of CAB-LA. Implementation research is needed to evaluate testing strategies, including the frequency and format of assays, while considering the intended use. Additional research is required to address concerns about HIV testing, including the potential role of HIV self-testing in optimizing testing frequency and follow-up after discontinuation. Studies are also needed to understand the factors contributing to breakthrough infections despite protective drug levels, which could inform the development of additional prevention strategies. Furthermore, as few cases of integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) resistance have been identified among individuals exposed to CAB-LA, further research is necessary to assess the levels and patterns of cross-resistance between cabotegravir (CAB) and dolutegravir (DTG). Oral PrEP has been delivered through various services, including those for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), sexual and reproductive health, antenatal and postnatal care, and primary healthcare, in settings such as clinics, pharmacies, and communities. Task-sharing among healthcare providers, including nurses and trained lay providers, has played an increasingly significant role in PrEP delivery. Differentiated PrEP delivery models support comprehensive, person-centered services tailored to the needs and preferences of individuals who could benefit from PrEP, thereby enhancing uptake, continuation, and effective use. To date, CAB-LA has only been implemented in trial settings. Implementation science is needed to evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of offering CAB-LA as an option alongside other PrEP methods and HIV prevention services across diverse settings and healthcare cadres. Concerns have been raised by PrEP providers that CAB-LA may lead to the re-medicalization of PrEP services, as many providers have experience delivering PrEP outside clinical settings, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. Research is needed to understand the perspectives and needs of providers implementing comprehensive PrEP services, including CAB-LA, and to assess potential regulatory restrictions that may limit the administration of CAB-LA injections by appropriately trained providers, including lay providers central to oral PrEP services. Implementation studies should explore strategies to optimize CAB-LA delivery alongside complementary services, such as contraceptive services and gender-affirming care, during the same clinic visit. Preliminary mathematical modeling suggests that increasing the total number of PrEP users, whether using oral PrEP or CAB-LA, has the greatest impact on reducing HIV incidence. CAB-LA use itself has the potential to avert additional HIV infections. Models for sub-Saharan Africa indicate that CAB-LA could be cost-effective even at a higher price than oral PrEP. However, further research is needed to assess the population-level impact, costs, and cost-effectiveness of CAB-LA across different settings and populations, using data from CAB-LA efficacy trials and implementation studies. Current models have largely considered extreme scenarios of PrEP scale-up and switching to CAB-LA; more realistic assumptions are required to inform programs on impact and cost-effectiveness. Additionally, no model has yet included a PrEP method mix that incorporates the dapivirine vaginal ring (DVR). Cost-effectiveness studies should also account for additional costs associated with CAB-LA, including those related to different HIV testing approaches and schedules. The WHO guideline on long-acting injectable cabotegravir for HIV prevention is being launched as a web-based product for dissemination and will include all evidence presented to the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The guideline will be incorporated into periodic updates of the WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV, which are informed by regular scoping exercises of available evidence and country implementation experiences. Dissemination efforts will include presentations at international conferences, workshops to support country adaptation, the development of adaptation tools to assist countries in prioritizing resource allocation, and briefings with international and national implementing partners. Data on policy and implementation changes will be made available through the WHO country intelligence database, updated every six months. The guideline development process adhered to WHO standards and involved systematic reviews of the safety, efficacy, and effectiveness of CAB-LA as PrEP, as well as reviews of values and preferences regarding injectable PrEP. The GRADE method was used to rate the quality of evidence and determine the strength of recommendations. The GDG reached consensus on the recommendations during virtual meetings, and the draft guidelines underwent peer review by the GDG and an External Review Group. Conflicts of interest were managed in accordance with WHO policy, and all declarations of interest are maintained on file for 10 years.
